verdict: Palo Alto Networks grew revenue 34% to $3.41B as its AI-security subscriptions surged, but one-time CyberArk deal charges flipped a $172M operating profit into a $282M net loss on paper.

segments.name: Subscription & support
segments.note: Security software subscriptions and support contracts — the recurring core, 78% of revenue, boosted by the CyberArk acquisition.

segments.name: Product
segments.note: Firewall hardware and appliances shipped to customers.

opex.name: Research & development
opex.note: Building the security platforms — swollen this quarter by the teams that came with CyberArk.

opex.name: Sales & marketing
opex.note: Selling security platforms to enterprises — the largest running cost.

opex.name: General & administrative
opex.note: Running the company day to day — jumped from $27M a year ago on CyberArk deal and integration costs.

takeaways.title: The platform bet is working
takeaways.text: Next-Generation Security ARR — subscriptions to its newer software platforms — grew 63% to $9.10B, adding nearly $1B in this single quarter.

takeaways.title: A paper loss, not a cash loss
takeaways.text: GAAP shows a $282M loss, driven by deal-related charges below the operating line. Operating cash flow was $1.4B in the same quarter — the loss consumed no cash.

takeaways.title: Future revenue is locked in
takeaways.text: Remaining performance obligations — contracted revenue not yet delivered — grew 34% to $21.2B, more than 6× this quarter's revenue.

oneTimers: The $441M other expense was mostly non-cash: fair-value changes on convertible notes acquired with CyberArk and the hedges against them. It is the entire reason a profitable operating quarter became a net loss.
G&A jumped to $226M from $27M a year ago on CyberArk acquisition and integration costs, including share-based pay tied to the deal.
Excluding one-offs and stock pay, Palo Alto earned $853M (non-GAAP) — the business itself was strongly profitable.
otherDetail: Other expense of $441M, net — mostly non-cash fair-value swings on convertible notes that came with the CyberArk acquisition, and related hedges.
follow100Note: Rows add up with a small rounding difference. Costs ran to $108.27 per $100 of revenue — the extra is the loss, covered by cash the company already had.
